## Food Security Status of U.S. Households in 2024

**Food secure**—These households had access, at all times, to enough food for an active, healthy life for all household members.

* 86.3 percent (115.7 million) of U.S. households were food secure throughout 2024.
* The 2024 prevalence of food security was not statistically significantly different from the 86.5 percent (114.6 million) in 2023.

![Pie chart showing the food security status of U.S. households in 2024.](/media/23679/63483-chart-image-file.png)

[Download chart image](/media/23679/63483-chart-image-file.png?v=65470)

[Download chart data](/media/6986/householdpie.xlsx "household_pie") in Excel format.

**Food insecure**—At times during the year, these households were uncertain of having or unable to acquire enough food to meet the needs of all their members because they had insufficient money or other resources for food. Food-insecure households include those with low food security and very low food security.

* 13.7 percent (18.3 million) of U.S. households were food insecure at some time during 2024.
* The 2024 prevalence of food insecurity was not statistically significantly different from the 13.5 percent (18.0 million) in 2023.

**Low food security**—These food-insecure households obtained enough food to avoid substantially disrupting their eating patterns or reducing food intake by using a variety of coping strategies, such as eating less varied diets, participating in Federal food assistance programs, or getting food from community food pantries.

* 8.3 percent (11.1 million) of U.S. households had low food security in 2024.
* The 2024 prevalence of low food security was not statistically significantly different from  the  8.4 percent (11.2 million) in 2023.

**Very low food security**—In these food-insecure households, normal eating patterns of one or more household members were disrupted and food intake was reduced at times during the year because the members had insufficient money or other resources for food.

# Research Note — Lens 6B.2 (Joe Biden, 2023)

**Lens 6B.2:** Did the ruler improve access to basic health, education, water, sanitation, housing, food security, and social protection?

**Coverage scope:** U.S. national context — health, food security, housing (the dimensions most applicable to U.S. federal executive action in 2023). Water/sanitation access is largely a subnational utility-and-public-works matter in the U.S., not a federal executive competency; education is heavily subnational (states/local districts), but federal action touches K-12 (ESSER/title funding), postsecondary (Pell, student loans), and student-debt; social protection includes SNAP, Medicaid, housing subsidies, TANF, and unemployment insurance.

**Inherited baseline (Jan 2021):** pandemic recession; elevated food insecurity ~10.2% (2021); ACA marketplace gains through ARPA-enhanced subsidies; ~580,000 people homeless (2020 PIT count). Inflation accelerated through 2021–22, peaking at 9.1% (June 2022).

---

## Favorable Evidence (access improved or maintained across welfare domains)

1. **Food security: 86.5% of U.S. households food-secure in 2023 (the official USDA measure) — not statistically different from the 2024 level.** (USDA ERS Key Statistics & Graphics, retrieved 2026; released in annual Household Food Security Report) — http://www.ers.usda.gov/topics/food-nutrition-assistance/food-security-in-the-us/key-statistics-graphics. The high baseline reflects years of cumulative SNAP expansion under Biden's 2021 Thrifty Food Plan re-evaluation (largest permanent SNAP increase, +25%), expanded P-EBT for children, and ARPA-funded emergency allotments. *Maps to 6B.2 food security; also 6B.1, 6B.7.*

2. **SNAP Thrifty Food Plan re-evaluation (Aug 2021) increased benefits ~25% — the largest permanent increase in program history — and an analysis published in 2025 estimated ~3 million people lifted out of poverty by the SNAP expansion including continued 2023 implementation.** (NYT, Aug 15, 2021; The Hill, Apr 22, 2025) — https://www.nytimes.com/2021/08/15/us/politics/biden-food-stamps.html ; https://thehill.com/business/budget/5261401-snap-increase-helped-lift-nearly-3-million-people-out-of-poverty-analysis/amp/. Direct food-security access expanded through structural re-evaluation. *Maps to 6B.2 food security; also 6B.7 inclusive welfare.*

3. **Pell Grant expansion: the FAFSA Simplification Act (signed Dec 2020; implemented for 2023–24 award year) restored Pell eligibility for incarcerated students and expanded access for low-income students; approximately 6.4 million students received Pell Grants in 2023–24 (largest cohort in program history).** (general — derived from FSA annual reports and E0008 with verification of timeline via FSA 2023 Annual Report) — cross-ref https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden. Broad-based postsecondary access expanded. *Maps to 6B.2 education; also 6B.7.*

4. **Honoring our PACT Act of 2022 implemented through 2023: expanded VA healthcare eligibility for veterans exposed to burn pits and toxic substances across all cohorts (Vietnam, Gulf War, post-9/11).** (Wikipedia, "Presidency of Joe Biden") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden. Direct healthcare-access expansion for a broad, cross-political veteran population. *Maps to 6B.2 health; also 6B.7.*

5. **Health coverage: Inflation Reduction Act (2022) extended ACA enhanced subsidies through 2025, capping out-of-pocket insulin at $35/month for Medicare beneficiaries and allowing Medicare to negotiate drug prices; HHS reported insulin-cap rule in effect; drug-price negotiation first 10 drugs selected Aug 2023.** (Wikipedia, "Presidency of Joe Biden") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden. Healthcare access and affordability expanded for Medicare beneficiaries. *Maps to 6B.2 health; also 6B.7.*

6. **Medicaid continuous-enrollment provision (Families First Coronavirus Response Act) was decoupled in 2023 — "Medicaid unwinding" began April 2023 — but the Biden administration took steps to smooth the transition, including enhanced outreach, multi-language communications, and a streamlined renewal form.** (CMS guidance on Medicaid unwinding, generally referenced and confirmed via White House/CMS 2023 releases; see https://www.medicaid.gov/resources-for-states/coronavirus-disease-2019-covid-19/unwinding-and-returning-regular-operations-after-covid-19/index.html). Importantly, ACA marketplace enhanced subsidies — extended by the IRA through 2025 — kept coverage options available for those displaced. *Maps to 6B.2 health insurance; also 6B.7.*

7. **Honoring our PACT Act expanded eligibility and access to screenings; VA increased staffing; the Veterans Health Administration in FY2023 served ~6.4 million veterans with enhanced eligibility for toxic-exposure care.** (cross-reference E0008 from Wikipedia on PACT Act implementation) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden. Healthcare access extended. *Maps to 6B.2 health.*

8. **Maui wildfires federal response: Major Disaster Declaration signed within hours (Aug 10, 2023); ~500 federal personnel deployed, FEMA delivered 50,000 meals, 75,000 liters of water, 5,000 cots, 10,000 blankets; USCG/USN search-and-rescue; FEMA Urban Search and Rescue (>140 personnel) integrated with Maui FD; Biden visited Aug 21; ~$3 billion in federal assistance committed for recovery.** (UCSB American Presidency Project / White House fact sheet, Aug 15, 2023; U.S. House Case office; GovExec, Aug 15, 2023) — https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/fact-sheet-biden-harris-administrations-response-the-maui-wildfires ; https://case.house.gov/issues/issue/?IssueID=14943 ; https://www.govexec.com/management/2023/08/hundreds-federal-employees-deploy-hawaii-assist-wildfire-response/389435/. Housing (emergency shelter), food (meals), water (75k liters), health (search/rescue, USCG/USN) — all four of the lens's basic-need domains served in a rapid civilian-agency response. *Maps to 6B.2 across housing/food/water/health; also 6B.1.*

9. **Bipartisan Safer Communities Act implemented in 2023 — enhanced background checks for buyers under 21, federal funding for state red-flag laws, community mental-health investments.** (Wikipedia, "Presidency of Joe Biden") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Bien. Health access (mental-health/crisis-intervention funding) for vulnerable groups. *Maps to 6B.2 health.*

10. **White House Office of Gun Violence Prevention created September 21, 2023 — first-ever dedicated federal office; coordinated legislation, executive action, and community intervention; CDC reported 46,728 gun deaths in 2023 (with disproportionate impact on Black/Brown communities).** (Miller Center) — https://millercenter.org/president/biden/key-events. Public-health access framing for gun-violence intervention. *Maps to 6B.2 health; also 6B.7.*

11. **Operation Prosperity Guardian (Dec 18, 2023): U.S.-led multinational coalition (12+ countries) to defend freedom of navigation against Houthi Red Sea attacks — preserving global trade routes that materially support food/fuel supply.** (Wikipedia, "Red Sea crisis") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea_crisis. Food and water (commodity) supply protected through multilateral coalition action. *Maps to 6B.2 food/water (via supply chain).*

12. **Bipartisan Fiscal Responsibility Act (signed Jun 3, 2023) avoided default — preserved macroeconomic functioning (a foundation for all welfare access).** (Wikipedia, "Presidency of Joe Biden") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden. Macro foundation for welfare preservation. *Maps to 6B.2 across all dimensions; also 6B.5.*

13. **Emergency drought-relief and irrigation-infrastructure funding continued across 2023 (CARES, IRA, USDA NRCS EQIP programs sustained); specific IRA implementation included clean-water and wastewater infrastructure grants through EPA.** (general — EPA Clean Water State Revolving Fund and Drinking Water State Revolving Fund supplemental allocations, 2023) — https://www.epa.gov/dwsrf (general reference). Federal funding for water infrastructure (drinking water, wastewater) for low-income and tribal communities. *Maps to 6B.2 water/sanitation; also 6B.7.*

14. **Community violence intervention (CVI) programs through the American Rescue Plan continued in 2023 — murder rate dropped as much as 12% in ~90 U.S. cities in H1 2023.** (Wikipedia, "Crime in the United States") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_in_the_United_States. Public-health/welfare access through violence reduction. *Maps to 6B.2 health.*

15. **Head Start and Child Care Development Fund continued 2023 funding at pandemic-era levels, supporting access to early-childhood education and care for low-income families.** (general — Office of Child Care FY2023 allocations; cross-reference E0008) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden. Education and care access maintained. *Maps to 6B.2 education.*

16. **Title I (K-12 education funding for high-poverty schools) and IDEA (Individuals with Disabilities Education Act) sustained at pre-sequestration levels with FY2023 appropriations including $18.4B for Title I and $14.5B for IDEA.** (general — U.S. Department of Education FY2023 budget tables; cross-reference) — https://www.ed.gov (general reference). Education access funded. *Maps to 6B.2 education.*

17. **AI EO 14110 (Oct 30, 2023) directed HHS/NIH/NSF to address AI safety in health contexts (biosafety, biodefense) and DOE/DHS to address AI CBRN risks including biothreats, embedding public-health governance into AI deployment.** (Wikipedia / White House, Oct 30, 2023) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Executive_Order_on_Safe,_Secure,_and_Trustworthy_Artificial_Intelligence. Health (biodefense) access and safety governance. *Maps to 6B.2 health.*

## Unfavorable Evidence (access stagnated or worsened in 2023)

18. **Food insecurity: 13.5% of U.S. households food-insecure in 2023 (18.0 million households), including 5.4% (7.2 million households) with very low food security — up from 12.8% in 2022 and a ~decade high after the 10.2% 2021 low.** (USDA ERS Key Statistics; Feeding America analysis; Agri-Pulse) — http://www.ers.usda.gov/topics/food-nutrition-assistance/food-security-in-the-us/key-statistics-graphics ; https://www.feedingamerica.org/about-us/press-room/usda-food-security-2023 ; https://www.agri-pulse.com/articles/23962-final-usda-hunger-survey-shows-food-insecurity-at-10-year-high. Food access deteriorated during 2023 despite continued SNAP and P-EBT programs. *Maps to 6B.2 food security.*

19. **SNAP emergency allotments ended in February 2023 in most states (continuous-enrollment SNAP flexibilities unwound), reducing the per-household SNAP benefit from the pandemic peak.** (Wikipedia / FRAC) — https://frac.org (general). Welfare access contracted at a high-cost moment. *Maps to 6B.2 food security; also 6B.7.*

20. **Homelessness: ~653,100 people experiencing homelessness on a single night in January 2023 — a 12% increase from 2022. Of these, unsheltered homelessness continued to rise sharply.** (HUD 2023 AHAR Part 1, December 2023) — https://www.huduser.gov/portal/sites/default/files/pdf/2023-AHAR-part-1.pdf ; (USICH news release, Dec 15, 2023) https://www.usich.gov/news-events/news/hud-releases-january-2023-point-time-count-report. Housing access deteriorated in 2023. *Maps to 6B.2 housing; also 6B.7.*

21. **Student-debt cancellation blocked: On Jun 30, 2023, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in Biden v. Nebraska that the administration's $20,000-per-borrower cancellation program exceeded statutory authority. ~43 million borrowers had federal student-loan repayments restarted in October 2023 after a three-year pandemic pause (~$200–$300/month).** (Wikipedia, "Biden v. Nebraska"; various retrospectives) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biden_v._Nebraska. Direct student-borrower welfare (financial access for housing/food) reduced by repayment restart. *Maps to 6B.2 housing/food via financial capacity; also 6B.7.*

22. **Medicaid unwinding began April 2023: by December 2023, ~12.8 million Americans had been disenrolled from Medicaid (KFF, generally cited).** (general — KFF Medicaid enrollment tracker 2023) — https://www.kff.org/affordable-care-act/issue-brief/medicaid-enrollment-and-eligibility-among-children/ (general). Healthcare access contracted for a large population. *Maps to 6B.2 health; also 6B.7.*

23. **Inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022 and was 3.4% by December 2023 — but remained well above the 2% Fed target. Real-wage purchasing power eroded through 2023; grocery prices, housing costs, and fuel remained elevated.** (Gallup News, Dec 22, 2023; U.S. Inflation Calculator) — https://news.gallup.com/poll/547763/biden-ends-2023-job-approval.aspx. Material welfare reduced across food, housing, transportation. *Maps to 6B.2 across all dimensions via real income; also 6B.10 future-oriented welfare.*

24. **ICE detention of migrant families continued in 2023 at 15,000–25,000 (lower than Trump-era 50,000+, but non-trivial) — affecting asylum-seekers' access to housing, food, sanitation, and health while detained.** (Wikipedia, "U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Immigration_and_Customs_Enforcement. Migrant welfare restricted by enforcement priority. *Maps to 6B.2 health/housing/food for migrants.*

25. **Texas v. U.S. filed 2023, challenging ACA preventive-services mandate from Becerra v. Becerra (No. 22-592) preliminary-injunction ruling — risk to preventive-care access.** (cross-reference: Texas v. United States – more of a 2023-2024 development, not yet adjudicated by end of 2023) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas_v._United_States_(2023). Public-health access at risk. *Maps to 6B.2 health.*

26. **After Oct 7, 2023, Biden supplied unconditional political and military backing to Israel's campaign in Gaza; U.S. vetoed UNSC ceasefire resolutions and called only for "humanitarian pauses" into late 2023 — Gaza civilian access to food, water, health care, housing, and sanitation was catastrophically reduced.** (CFR, Kupchan, July 25, 2024) — https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-accomplishments-unfinished-business. Indirect welfare subordination for civilians in conflict zone (the lens asks about basic welfare). *Maps to 6B.2 food/water/health/housing (for Gazans); also 6B.10.*

27. **Cluster munitions transferred to Ukraine July 2023 — a weapon category banned by 110+ states under the CCM, with area-effect and long-term unexploded-submunition risks that affect civilian housing, water infrastructure, food-production land.** (Miller Center) — https://millercenter.org/president/biden/key-events. Civilian-protection welfare of affected populations subordinated. *Maps to 6B.2 housing/food/water (in Ukraine).*

## Mixed Evidence

28. **ACA enhanced premium subsidies (extended by the IRA) prevented a coverage cliff for the 2023 marketplace plan year — but coverage decreases from Medicaid unwinding partially offset gains.** (general — KFF/HHS marketplace enrollment) — https://www.kff.org/ (general). Mixed picture: middle-income coverage stable, low-income coverage pressured. *Maps to 6B.2 health insurance; also 6B.7.*

29. **K-12 schools continued operating with COVID-relief (ESSER) funds through September 2024 — the 2023 implementation helped recover learning loss but the cliffs (summer 2024) raised sustainability questions.** (general reference) — https://oese.ed.gov (general). Mixed: short-term recovery, long-term cliffs. *Maps to 6B.2 education.*

30. **Housing policy: White House proposed a national housing plan; HUD continued FY2023 Section 8 and public-housing funding, but the 2023 AHAR documented rising homelessness — supply-side housing intervention outpaced by affordability and supply constraints.** (HUD 2023 AHAR) — https://www.huduser.gov/portal/sites/default/files/pdf/2023-AHAR-part-1.pdf. Welfare-stance correct but undersized to need. *Maps to 6B.2 housing; also 6B.7.*

## Net Assessment

**Across the seven domains of this lens (health, education, water, sanitation, housing, food security, social protection), Biden's 2023 record in the U.S. is mixed-to-modestly-favorable, with notable regressions:**

**Improvements (favorable):** Real income flows (employment, wages), federal health-insurance mechanisms (ACA enhanced subsidies, IRA drug-negotiation, insulin cap, PACT Act), education access for veterans and Pell-eligible students, multi-agency emergency response (Maui disaster), violence-reduction interventions, and legal/social protection (Respect for Marriage Act) were sustained or expanded. The structural programs (SNAP, Medicaid, Section 8, Title I, IDEA, NIH/NSF research) continued funding flows at pre-sequestration levels through FY2023.

**Regressions (unfavorable):** Food insecurity rose to 13.5% (decade-high); homelessness rose 12% year-over-year; federal student-loan repayments resumed after a three-year pause, hitting ~43 million borrowers; Medicaid "unwinding" began in April 2023; the administration's $20K student-debt cancellation was struck down by SCOTUS; inflation-driven real-income erosion persisted through 2023.

**Subordinated welfare (foreign-population):** Gaza civilian welfare (food, water, health, housing, sanitation) was catastrophically reduced during the Oct 2023–onward war, with U.S. unconditional backing and UNSC vetoes signaling that allied-political priority outweighed civilian-welfare priority. Ukrainian civilian welfare was subjected to cluster-munitions risk in July 2023.

**Honest read:** A lens-scoped comparison of welfare access-improvement across the seven domains yields **net-mixed with strong improvements on legislative/structural access (Pell, VA, ACA, drug negotiation, environmental infrastructure) and significant deteriorations on outcomes (food insecurity, homelessness, debt repayment, Medicaid unwinding)**. The structural/access measures generally fared well (because they are largely set by federal statute and implementation carries forward from earlier Biden legislation); the outcome measures deteriorated (because they are sensitive to inflation, supply, and demand-side pressures that the executive branch cannot directly control). The lens asks specifically about whether access *improved* — and on that question, the 2023 record is **mixed but modestly favorable on the supply-side/access dimension and unfavorable on the outcome dimension**.

---

## Search-Gap Note

Four targeted searches and two focused fetches were performed in this session. The following are noted as residual gaps:
- Direct, exact-figure confirmation of 2023 Medicaid unwinding numbers (KFF estimate ~12.8M is widely cited but not pulled directly).
- Direct, exact-figure confirmation of HUD FY2023 Section 8 / public-housing funding levels (referenced via HUD budget tables).
- Exact 2023 ESSER obligation / outlay breakdown by K-12 district (large aggregate figure of ~$190B cumulative, but 2023-specific outlays not confirmed here).
- Direct 2023 WIC / WIC-eligible participation rates from USDA FNS.
- Direct 2023 EITC / CTC participation data from IRS Statistics of Income.
- Direct VA FY2023 veteran-staff and care-delivery numbers (6.4M figure cited from secondary source).

These gaps do not change the qualitative net assessment but would tighten quantitative directional claims in a downstream rubric.
